newsitem.title: PERU: Mother says proud of dead Peruvian rebel leader.
newsitem.headline: Mother says proud of dead Peruvian rebel leader.

text.p: The mother of Peruvian rebel leader Nestor Cerpa, who died during the bloody hostage rescue at the Japanese ambassador's residence, said on Wednesday she was proud of her son and hoped to go to Peru to bury him.

"Everything that has happened seems unreal to me. But I am proud of my son as he has died giving his blood, his life for his comrades," Felicita Cartolini said in comments to Peruvian television from her home in Nantes, France.
"He wanted to rescue all his jailed comrades."

Cerpa and 13 of his fellow Tupac Amaru Revolutionary (MRTA) fighters died on Tuesday after Peru's crack commanders stormed the home where they had been holding 72 hostages since Dec. 17 demanding the release of around 450 imprisoned rebels.

The guerrilla's mother said she now feared for the safety of Nestor's wife Nancy Gilvonio who is serving a life sentence for "terrorism" in a top-security jail in the Andean highlands near Puno in southern Peru.
Cartolini, who lives in a poor neighbourhood in Nantes, looks after the couple's two young children.

She said she wanted to travel to Peru to bury her 43-year old son who had been involved in guerrilla movements since the early 1980s. "I want to bury my son and see him for one last time," said Cartolini, her voice trembling with emotion.
"This morning I spoke to the Red Cross and they are going to make the arrangements to see if I can see him for the last time."
Friends and former comrades said Cerpa was not a violent man but a shy cautious thinker committed to leftist revolution. He favoured books over bullets and dialogue to death, they said.
"The members of the revolutionary command were careful to respect the hostages without maltreating them, humiliating them. Rather they knew how to live with them," Cerpa's mother said.
The hostage-takers were caught off guard by the meticulously planned attack that surprised the mainly teenage guerrillas as they played soccer in one of the diplomatic mansion's reception rooms.
The assault, which also cost the lives of one hostage and two soldiers, was an act of "duplicity and treason" by President Alberto Fujimori, Cartolini said in comments to French television.
"The Peruvian state has not respected this peaceful movement and has killed with great cruelty without respect for life."
